nodes.question: What advancements have been made in the field of fluid solid coupling mechanics?
nodes.answer: There have been significant advancements in understanding the quantitative correlation between temperature fluctuations and high-cycle thermal fatigue.
nodes.paragraph: As previously stated, engineers and researchers are becoming increasingly concerned with the mixing behaviours and temperature uctuations in the T-section because they can cause thermal fatigue and damage. Hence,a potential correlation could exist between uctuations intemperature and thermal fatigue. Furthermore, the degree of uctuation of temperature can serve as a qualitative indi- cator for estimating high-cycle thermal fatigue. Numerousresearchers have utilized the Power Spectral Density and Root Mean Square to quantify the amplitude and frequency of the uctuation, respectively, when assessing thermalfatigue and temperature uctuations in T-sections [ 6,13]. Based on the aforementioned mechanism and research approach, numerous researchers [ 14 16] reported that cram- ming porous medium in the interfacial zone was helpful inthe reduction of thermal uctuations in the T-section. nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What is the new alloy composition synthesized in this study?
nodes.answer: The new alloy composition synthesized is Fe10Cr1Ti3AI6, which was created by substituting Fe with Cr in Fe11Ti3AI6.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract In general, any attempt to increase the Seebeck coefficient is usually accompanied by a decrease in the electrical conductiv - ity or vice versa due to the interplay between these two parameters. This work demonstrates that a simultaneous increase in both the Seebeck coefficient and electrical conductivity can be obtained by doping in intermetallic alloys. A new alloy composition, Fe10Cr1Ti3AI6, was synthesized by substituting Fe with Cr in Fe11Ti3AI6 using mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The thermoelectric measurements revealed that the Cr substitution led to an increase in the Seebeck coefficient from +27 V/K in Fe11Ti3AI6 to +39 V/K in Fe10Cr1Ti3Al6, with a corresponding increase in the electrical conductivity from 2.5 105 S/m to 4.7 105 S/m, resulting in a significant increase in the power factor. The temperature dependence of the thermoelectric properties of this new alloy was also investigated over a temperature range of 50 727 C. The result showed that a maximum power factor of 6.0 10 4 W/m K2 was obtained at 53 C. Keywords Intermetallic powder metallurgy thermoelectric ball milling spark plasma sintering Introduction A continuous increase in the global energy demand has been seen over the past few decades.

nodes.question: What is the primary focus of the study regarding Thermal Frontal Polymerization (TFP) in the context of polymer composites?
nodes.answer: The study focuses on the numerical simulation of TFP in Bisphenol A Diglycidyl Ether (BADGE) composites filled with Fe3O4 nanoparticles, particularly examining the effects of different filling degrees on the key characteristics of the TFP process.
nodes.paragraph: No Title Available DOI: DOI not available FullTextURL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10443-025-10309-5 RESEARCHReceived: 24 June 2024 / Accepted: 16 January 2025 The Author(s) 2025 Margit Lang margit.lang@pccl.at 1 Polymer Competence Center Leoben GmbH (PCCL), Sauraugasse 1, Leoben 8700, Austria 2 Montanuniversitaet Leoben, Chair of Designing Plastics and Composite Materials, Leoben 8700, Austria 3 Institute for Chemistry and Technology of Materials, University of Technology of Graz, NAWI Graz, Stremayrgasse 9, Graz 8010, AustriaThermal Frontal Polymerization in Polymer Composites: Numerical Simulation and the Role of Fe3O4 Nanoparticle Fillers Margit Lang1,2 Christoph Schmidleitner1,3 Venu Prakash Kasinikota1 Elisabeth Rossegger1Applied Composite Materials https://doi.org/10.1007/s10443-25-10309-5 Abstract Recently Thermal Frontal Polymerization (TFP) has emerged as a low-energy alternative, that enables rapid and energy-efficient manufacturing of composites. Thus, compared to conventional processes, this innovative curing and polymerization process exhibits im - proved efficiency and reduced environmental impact and provides a promising strategy to address sustainability challenges. However, successful TFP requires a delicate balance of reaction rates, exothermicity, and efficient heat transport into unpolymerized media while minimizing heat losses to the surroundings.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean energy|Wind turbines|Advances in wind turbine materials_qna_005
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What is the main focus of the study mentioned in the paragraph regarding Badges and Fe3O4 nanoparticles?
nodes.answer: The study focuses on the impact of different filling degrees of Fe3O4 nanoparticle fillers on the thermal frontal polymerization (TFP) process of Bisphenol A Diglycidyl Ether (BADGE) resin, specifically investigating how these fillers influence curing kinetics and thermal transport characteristics.
nodes.paragraph: In this context, sustaining TFP of polymers reinforced with highly conductive fillers is challenging due to the increased energy dis - sipation and reduced availability of exothermic energy as the filler content increases at the cost of resin volume. In this work, a numerical study of the TFP based manufacturing of Bisphenol A Diglycidyl Ether (BADGE) filled with Fe3O4 nanoparticles is presented. The simulation provides insight into the thermo-chemical process and into the impact of different particle filling degrees on the key characteristics of TFP, i.e., maximum attainable degree of cure, maximum temperature, front shape, and front speed. Keywords Thermal frontal polymerization (TFP) Polymer composites Nanoparticle fillers Polymerization 1 3 Applied Composite Materials Introduction Given the global priority of sustainability and waste reduction, polymer composites play an important role in enabling high-performance, lightweight structures and increasing product lifespans by decades due to corrosion resistance and durability. At the same time, innova - tive curing and polymerization processes must exhibit improved efficiencies and reduced environmental impact [ 1]. In this context, Frontal Polymerization (FP) has emerged as a low-energy alternative that enables rapid and energy-efficient manufacturing of composites compared to conventional processes, thus providing a promising strategy to address sustain - ability challenges [ 2].

nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What is the main focus of the study discussed in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: The study focuses on the Thermal Frontal Polymerization (TFP) of Bisphenol A Diglycidyl Ether (BADGE) reinforced with Fe3O4 nanoparticles, specifically examining how different filling degrees of these nanoparticles affect the polymerization process.
nodes.paragraph: Frontal Polymerization (FP) is a technique that harnesses the chemi - cal energy stored within a resin to drive material synthesis. In this self-sustained process, an initial stimulus (e.g., thermal or photo) induces a localized reaction zone, the so-called polymerization front , which can propagate through the entire system without requiring further energy input. For instance, in Thermal Frontal Polymerization (TFP) the heat, i.e., the thermal trigger, is only applied to a small area of the sample and for a time interval that is short compared to the total cure time, see Fig. 1. The local increase in temperature triggers the polymerization of the reactants. Subsequently, the heat released by the curing process is transferred to the surrounding regions, promoting the creation of a hot reaction front that propagates to the unreacted regions of the reactants, thus converting them into polymer. TFP is the most widely studied mechanism, having the widest range of velocities, rates of conversion, and types of materials that can be used [ 3]. In general, FP requires highly exothermic polymerization processes, as well as efficient heat transport within the monomer solution for front propagation.

nodes.question: How does the incorporation of Fe3O4 nanoparticles influence the frontal polymerization process according to the text?
nodes.answer: The incorporation of Fe3O4 nanoparticles affects the thermal transport characteristics and the curing behavior, leading to challenges such as increased energy dissipation, reduced heat generation, and a decline in frontal velocity and temperature as the filler content increases.

nodes.question: What are the challenges associated with sustaining Thermal Frontal Polymerization (TFP) in polymers reinforced with highly conductive fillers?
nodes.answer: The challenges include increased energy dissipation and reduced availability of exothermic energy as the filler content increases, which comes at the cost of reducing the resin volume.
nodes.paragraph: The efficacy of heat trans - port through the unpolymerized medium is determined by the thermal conductivity and heat capacity of the reaction media [ 4]. Furthermore, boundary condition effects like heat loss to the surrounding medium can have a significant influence, i.e., can alter the thermal equilibrium between the heat generated by the exothermic reaction and the heat consumed by the advancing front [ 4, 5]. Motivated by the substantial energy and time savings offered by the FP approach, com - pared to conventional manufacturing techniques, more advances have been made in the development and usage of this technique for the rapid fabrication of reinforced, highly filled polymer composites [ 2, 4, 6 9]. nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean energy|Wind turbines|Advances in wind turbine materials_qna_010
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What is the main focus of the study involving Bisphenol A Diglycidyl Ether (BADGE) and Fe3O4 nanoparticle fillers?
nodes.answer: The study focuses on the effects of different filling degrees of Fe3O4 nanoparticle fillers on the curing kinetics and thermal front propagation during Radical-Induced Cationic Frontal Polymerization (RICFP) of BADGE resin.
nodes.paragraph: Given the fact, that in TFP the polymerization is driven by a thermal front, the thermal conductivity of the reinforcing phase along with the reduced resin content is a crucial factor in understanding and controlling the reaction. The incorporation of highly conductive fillers alters the thermal transport characteristics during FP and it may allow heat from the polym - erization reaction to advance ahead of the front into the unreacted monomer, like experi - mentally and numerically shown by Goli et al. [ 5] for continuous conductive elements. Tran et al. [ 3] successfully evaluated the influence of various types of fillers (e.g., aluminium, glass microspheres, graphite, mica, ) on the FP behavior of a BADGE-based system. The authors found that the reduction in monomer fraction led to a reduction in heat generation, while the fillers also absorbed parts of heat, resulting in a declined frontal velocity and tem - perature with increasing filler content. Instabilities in FP due to the addition of fillers, i.e., an increased energy dissipation and reduced availability of exothermic energy as the volume fraction of the resin decreases with increasing filler content, were also reported by Suslick et at [ 4].

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean energy|Wind turbines|Advances in wind turbine materials_qna_011
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What is the primary focus of the research conducted by Margit Lang and colleagues regarding polymer composites?
nodes.answer: The research primarily focuses on the numerical study of Thermal Frontal Polymerization (TFP) in Bisphenol A Diglycidyl Ether (BADGE) filled with Fe3O4 nanoparticles, examining the impact of different particle filling degrees on TFP characteristics.
nodes.paragraph: Further efforts to study the effects of added fillers (glass, steel, carbon) include the publications of Kumar et al. [ 6] who presented analytical expressions for the velocity of the self-propagating reaction front in the FP of thermoset polymers and composites, Vyas et al. [10] who presented a numerical study of the manufacturing of unidirectional glass-fiber- reinforced composites via FP, Wang et al. [ 9] who investigated the effect of fiber volume fraction on the average front velocity and the maximum temperature in the FP process, and Centellas et al. [ 10] who investigated the effect of multiple polymerization fronts on the composite cure time, quality, and mechanical performance. However, the detailed investi - gation of the influence of different filling degrees (in particular with respect to composites with high filling degrees on inorganic particles) using mathematical modeling & numerical simulation routines, is still in its infancy. With respect to curing kinetics, publications are either based on the determination of cur - ing kinetics of the unfilled resin, ignoring the influence of the filler content on curing kinet - ics, e.g., by Wang et al.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean energy|Wind turbines|Advances in wind turbine materials_qna_012
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What is the primary purpose of using Fe3O4 nanoparticles in the Thermal Frontal Polymerization (TFP) of Bisphenol A Diglycidyl Ether (BADGE)?
nodes.answer: The primary purpose of using Fe3O4 nanoparticles is to modify the properties of the composite, particularly through their unique characteristics such as superparamagnetism and high surface-to-volume ratio, which can enhance the thermal transport characteristics and curing behavior in TFP.
nodes.paragraph: [ 11] and Centellas et al. [ 8] or provide a systematic experimental investigation of the influence of predefined filler content and/or filler shape on curing kinet - ics [12 14]. However, no studies on studies on Bisphenol A Diglycidyl Ether (BADGE) with different filling degrees of Fe3O4 nanoparticles can be found in literature. In this study, Fe3O4 nanoparticle fillers were added to a Bisphenol A Diglycidyl Ether (BADGE) resin system that frontally polymerized through a Radical-Induced Cationic Frontal Polymerization (RICFP) mechanism. The nano-size Fe3O4 is an attractive material due to its unique characteristic properties such as superparamagnetism, low toxicity, high surface to volume ratio, easy synthesis, and biocompatibility [ 15]. An application field of such magnetic composite materials is electromagnetic shielding, which aims at reducing the electromagnetic field in defined areas. The detailed compilation of fundamental material and their subsequent usage in Modeling & Simulation routines is expected to be a major contribution in the investigation of the various parameters that influence the dynamic phe - nomenon of FP and can support process optimization.
